To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 3 potential power analyses.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8’ to check the contents of 10 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: sample_size, alpha_level, power, effect_size, effect_size_metric, software

power_id text
1 There is however reason to believe that mediation analysis is not always conducted in a completely a priori manner, which has serious consequences for the validity of the reported has only been used to examine mediation analyses. It was developed to evaluate evidential value from sets of statistical tests which primarily use confidence intervals (rather than p-values), and this measure requires additional validation, which we provide in Study 1. Study 1 uses a Monte Carlo simulation study to demonstrate how flexibility in mediation analysis can manifest in false-positive rates far greater than the nominal 𝛼𝛼 level and this inflated false-positive rate is reflected accurately by the RP index. Study 2 compares the distribution of published mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology with simulations of mediation analyses at different levels of statistical power. Our results indicate that mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology research are typically underpowered and/or show signs of selective reporting, which substantially limits the evidential value of the literature. We conclude by discussing ways to improve the evidential value of mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology research.
2 We ran a series of simulations to determine how the RP scores ought to be distributed for simple mediation analyses when adequately powered (80-95% power), low-powered (33-79% power), and null effects (~5% false-positive rate). We used the simstudy::genCorData R function (Goldfield & Wjciak-Jens, 2019) to create each simulated dataset with pre-specified population-level correlations among the three variables (X, the independent variable; M, the mediator, and Y, the outcome variable). To test the simulated indirect effects, we used the mediate function from the psych package for R (Revelle, 2015) with default options (alpha = .05; 5,000 bootstraps; percentile CIs). We verified that this tool gives results consistent with the PROCESS macro (Hayes, 2022). Just like with the test statistics collected from marketing and consumer psychology journals, RP scores were calculated using Equation 1.
3 All simulations were designed such that the RP > 0 peak of their respective RP distributions matched the peak of the marketing and consumer psychology journals’ RP distribution. 5 This allowed us to compare the shapes of the simulated and observed distributions directly using absolute frequencies. In our final simulated distributions, mediation analyses reached statistical significance in 87% (a<b), 89% (a=b), and 89% (a > b) of tests designed to simulate adequate power, 58% (a<b), 60% (a=b), and 60% (a > b) of tests simulating low power.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 242 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: R history (2), RStudio session files (240). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 12 distinct packages/libraries: beepr, dplyr, ggplot2, jtools, lavaan, mosaic, psych, purrr, readxl, simstudy, tidyr, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

Resolved 10.1002/jcpy.1117 Disconfirming Expectations: Incorrect Imprecise (vs. Precise) Estimates Increase Source Trustworthiness and Consumer Loyalty Journal of Consumer Psychology Pena-Marin 2019 When trustworthiness in the realtor was included in the model as the mediator, the analysis yielded a positive effect (b = .47, SE = 0.20) that was statistically different from zero (CI: 0.08 to 0.87). Resolved 10.1093/jcr/ucy059 Room for Opportunity: Resource Scarcity Increases Attractiveness of Range Marketing Offers Journal of Consumer Research Fan 2019 Mediation analyses confirmed that the effect of resource scarcity on attitude toward the range offer was mediated by participants’ promotion orientation. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 260 columns across 12 data files.

Issues Identified

60 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • data_simulations_and_reported.R reads P-Curve Consumer Behavior Data.xlsx.
  • JPSP Analysis.R reads mediation-tests-jpsp.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • RDFsimulation.R
  • data_simulations_extension.R
  • Study2_data_simulations_analysis.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Calls that install packages in the code

2 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

library() calls added

1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself. The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run it we added the library() calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after adding library() calls it should make itself.

> cigap <- function(lowci, hici){
>   truelow <- min(lowci,hici)
>   truehigh <- max(lowci,hici)
>   gapwidth <- truehigh - truelow
>   absolutecigap <- min(abs(truelow),abs(truehigh))/gapwidth
>   if(truehigh * truelow >= 0){
>     return(absolutecigap)
>   }
>   else{
>     return(-absolutecigap)
>   }
> }

The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

4 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook files bundle the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the files itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 64 result tables (92 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.
