How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

:::

Full text

Abstract

Mediation analysis plays a central role in marketing research and consumer psychology by modeling the complex processes underlying total effects. Like other inferential methods, tests of indirect effects are susceptible to false-positive results when multiple defensible analytic decisions can lead to different conclusions (i.e. researcher degrees of freedom). To assess the collective evidential value of mediation analyses in marketing, we (1) measure the relative proximity (RP) of confidence intervals to zero and (2) aggregate a related set of RP scores into a single distribution. Study 1 demonstrates how researcher degrees of freedom in mediation analysis, such as trying many different mediators and outcomes or testing moderated mediation, can inflate false-positive rates to up to 20% in the scenarios we examined. This study also demonstrates the validity of the RP index by examining its correspondence with false-positive findings. In Study 2, we compare the RP distribution of mediation analyses published in top marketing journals (2018-2020) to simulations of null effects, low power, and adequate power.

We find that mediation analyses in marketing substantially deviated from simulations with adequate power but were similar to simulated distributions with low power and null effects. We propose study preregistration, increased statistical power, and reduction of selection bias as solutions to increase evidential value of mediation analyses going forward.

Keywords: mediation analysis, p-hacking, researcher degrees of freedom, moderated mediation, process analysis, indirect effect results. Some mediation analyses may have been specified post hoc, although the analysis tools, like most inferential approaches, are designed to test preplanned hypotheses. Pham and Oh (2021), argued that "most consumer research should probably be regarded as exploratory" (p. 168) and argued that, due to their complexity, we shouldn't expect mediation models to be specified a priori. Adding further evidence that mediation analyses, as they are currently implemented, may not be truly confirmatory though they are customarily reported as such.

Janiszewski and van Osselaer (2021) provided survey data showing that only 25% of consumer research studies are purely deductive, meaning that exploration and post hoc testing play a role in the remaining 75% of studies. Additionally, some methods papers actually advocate for testing many different mediation models to identify the "true mediator" (Fiedler, Harris, & Schott, 2018, p. 96;Fiedler, Schott, & Meiser, 2011) or to find the true direction of causality (Wiedermann & von Eye, 2015). These results cumulatively suggest that mediation analysis may be subject to selective reporting, which is when researchers share only certain findings or outcomes based on characteristics of the results (e.g., statistical significance, direction). In this paper, we demonstrate how these practices can inflate false-positive error rates, which threatens the evidential value of the collective literature. A literature or set of findings is said to have evidential value when selective reporting can be ruled out as the sole explanation for those findings (Simonsohn, et al. 2014). Misrepresentation of data exploration as confirmatory research and formal calls for systematic multiple testing may lead to inflated false-positive error rates through selective reporting, reducing evidential value. This manuscript seeks to assess the evidential value of mediation analyses published in four high impact marketing and consumer psychology journals using a measure called relative proximity (RP;Götz et al., 2021). RP has only been applied in one study (Götz et al., 2021), and

Introduction

One of the core objectives of marketing research and consumer psychology is to go beyond an observable phenomenon and tap into the underlying processes (Holbrook & Batra, 1987; Sujan, 1985). Behavioral interventions, for instance, often affect choices through cognitive processes. Mediation analysis allows researchers to test the consistency of observed data with hypothesized causal mechanisms and estimate the extent to which the total effect of a manipulation on an outcome variable is explained by a proposed mechanism, a mediator. The generated insights are relevant for marketing and consumer psychology researchers for both theory testing and application. For example, Li, Yin, and Xu (2026) found that in fundraising, when total goal amount (e.g., $6,400) is divisible by individual contribution request (e.g., $8), individuals are more likely to contribute, and that this effect is mediated by perceived clarity of the individual's contribution. Their model applies theory from research on numerical cognition and collective goals, but it also identifies a practical mechanism by which other approaches to increasing donations could operate. Mediation analysis has thus been increasingly used to deepen the understanding of the observed phenomena and heighten the relevance of the research. A review of papers in the Journal of Consumer Research in 2014-2016 found 71% of articles with experiments included a mediation analysis (Pieters, 2017). In our own analysis, about half (47%) of all articles published in major marketing and consumer psychology journals contain a mediation analysis. This enormous popularity is at least partially driven by the accessibility of software to estimate and conduct inference on indirect effects (e.g., the PROCESS macro, Hayes, 2022).

There is however reason to believe that mediation analysis is not always conducted in a completely a priori manner, which has serious consequences for the validity of the reported has only been used to examine mediation analyses. It was developed to evaluate evidential value from sets of statistical tests which primarily use confidence intervals (rather than p-values), and this measure requires additional validation, which we provide in Study 1. Study 1 uses a Monte Carlo simulation study to demonstrate how flexibility in mediation analysis can manifest in false-positive rates far greater than the nominal 𝛼𝛼 level and this inflated false-positive rate is reflected accurately by the RP index. Study 2 compares the distribution of published mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology with simulations of mediation analyses at different levels of statistical power. Our results indicate that mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology research are typically underpowered and/or show signs of selective reporting, which substantially limits the evidential value of the literature. We conclude by discussing ways to improve the evidential value of mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology research.

Mediation Analysis in Marketing and Consumer Psychology Journals

As most commonly used in consumer psychology and marketing research, a mediation analysis is a regression-based statistical model used to assess whether a proposed mediator (M) could be part of a causal chain between X and Y, such that X affects M which then affects Y (See Figure 1). For example, Shaddy and colleagues (2026) found that consumers showed lower support of brands (Y) that used demographic targeting of advertisements (as compared to broad advertisements; X), and that this effect was mediated by appraisals of discrimination (M).

Mediation analysis is appealing because it can broaden the field's theoretical understanding of the effect itself by exploring why or how an effect occurs. Additionally, identification of mediators provides greater opportunity to capitalize on this mechanism through other antecedent variables. through M.

Importantly, mediation analysis only analyzes covariance and does not provide evidence for causality. Causality must be established through experimental design and theory (Hayes, 2022; Imai, Tingley, Yamamoto, 2013; Pieters, 2017; Rohrer et al., 2022). Caution is required when interpreting mediation results to clarify the distinction between results being consistent with a proposed causal model compared to evidence for the causal model itself. Apart from a false-positive result, a significant indirect effect can also be the result of response style bias that affects the involved variables (e.g., acquiescence, midpoint responding; Baumgartner and Steenkamp 2001), "meaningless mediation" where M is really a different measure of Y or a manipulation check (Lynch, 2011; Zhao, Lynch, & Chen 2010), demand effects, confounds, or other problems (MacKinnon et al., 2000). Researchers using mediation analysis have frequently been critiqued for generating causal claims that are unfounded, underreporting causal identification assumptions which clarify issues around confounding and temporal ordering (Imai et al., 2010; Tate, 2015; Vo et al., 2020). While confounding can bias a point estimate, even in causal mediation approaches that attempt to address these biases, confidence interval approaches are used for making statistical inference. Even the absence of confounding biases and perfect application of causal inference approaches (which primarily are about textual interpretations and assumption transparency), would not remove the issue this manuscript focuses on: bias in reporting and conduct of mediation analysis based on preference for statistically significant effects.

A few marketing scholars have ably argued for a more colorful palette of epistemological and methodological approaches to marketing and consumer psychology research exploring mechanisms (Inman et al., 2018; Lynch et al., 2012; Pham, 2013; Peracchio, Luce, & McGill, 2014). But mediation analysis continues to play a prominent role in many leading marketing and consumer psychology journals (Pieters, 2017). This is true of experimental consumer psychology, but also of other adjacent sub-fields of marketing. This powerful push for process evidence has even spilled over into consumer culture theory, where researchers increasingly use qualitative methods to understand consumer processes (e.g., "hegemonic memory making" Brunk, Giesler, & Hartmann, 2017; Giesler & Thompson, 2016). Indeed, with the few exceptions of modeling and quantitative review papers, one is hard-pressed to find empirical papers that lack mediation analyses. In our own review, we found that of 647 papers in the top four marketing and consumer psychology journals in 2018 -2020, 308 (47.6%) contained at least one mediation analysis.

Statistical inference for the indirect effect of X on Y through M is different from other standard approaches since the indirect effect is the product of the estimated effects of X on M (𝑎𝑎) and M on Y controlling for X (𝑎𝑎). The indirect effect has an unusual sampling distribution, where the shape and spread is dependent on the population values of the a and b paths separately. Null hypothesis significance testing is difficult in the context of mediation because there is no single null distribution for the indirect effect (Tofighi, 2020), thus reporting p-values for tests of mediation is relatively rare. As a consequence, the indirect effect (𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎) is typically reported with a confidence interval (CI). There exist many different methods to generate the confidence interval around an indirect effect. Currently, bootstrap confidence intervals for the indirect effect, as proposed by Shrout and Bolger (2002), are the preferred method of inference with the most common tool being the PROCESS macro (Hayes, 2022). Bootstrapping methods outperform methods that assume a normal sampling distribution by having higher statistical power and more appropriate false-positive error rates (Biesanz, Falk, & Savalei, 2010; Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007; MacKinnon, Lockwood, & Williams, 2004).

The CI can be used to determine statistical significance: Consider for example, a 95% CI of [0.01, 0.03]. In this example the coefficient is deemed statistically significant at 𝛼𝛼 = .05 level, because the 95% CI does not include zero. But, from this interval, we cannot tell if the coefficient is significant at 𝛼𝛼 = 0.01. This leaves a gap between what could be known with a pvalue compared to a bootstrap CI, because readers cannot know whether an effect would be significant at any level other than what is reported. This issue is somewhat unique to bootstrap CIs, as with parametric CIs it is typically possible to back-calculate the standard error and generate all possible CIs or p-values.

The Evidential Value in Mediation Analyses

Preregistering, or preplanning a mediation analysis may pose difficulties to some researchers, since it requires a deeper understanding of the structure of the data compared to preregistering the hypotheses and procedures for testing a total effect. But deciding on the analysis post hoc increases the risk that decisions are guided by potentially random patterns in the data (Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven, & Mellor, 2018). When comparing dissertations to publications in management research, researchers often add/drop data, covariates, and hypotheses before publishing in peer-reviewed journals (Kepes et al., 2022). This problem, well known from other analyses, is aggravated in the case of mediation analyses since the analyses allow for a large number of configurations that offer many researcher degrees of freedom (Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn, 2011). Moreover, while replication studies are increasingly conducted in marketing and consumer psychology to add evidential value for an established effect, replications typically focus on total effects instead of indirect effects.

Given the prominence and relevance of mediation analyses in marketing it is important to evaluate the evidential value using the information that is reported in mediation analyses. The lack of p-values-specifically the lack of a standard approach for calculating the p-value of indirect effects-constrains the application of existing methods that have been developed to assess the evidential value in a set of empirical findings (e.g., Simonsohn et al. 2014; but see Morey & Davis-Stober, 2026). To that goal we refer to a more recently developed method that estimates evidential value based on the ratio of a CI's distance to zero and the width of the CI (Götz et al., 2021). The distance, the ratio's numerator, is a function of the size of the effect, while the width of the CI, the denominator, indicates uncertainty in the estimate. Thus, larger ratios indicate stronger evidence.

Following this reasoning, Götz and colleagues (2021) call this ratio the "relative proximity" of the CI to zero (RP). If CIs are systematically too close to zero it is indicative of low evidential value like what is signaled by p-values that are systematically too close to .05.

Thus, when applied to mediation analysis this test statistic divides the distance to zero of an indirect effect's CI by the range of the CI. RP can be mathematically represented as a function of the upper bound of the CI (𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 ) and the lower bound of the CI (𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 ), where the 𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠 function indicates the mathematical sign of a number:

This equation breaks down the distance of the CI from zero, min��𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 �, |𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 |�, whether it is positive or negative, and scales by the width of the CI, 𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 -𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 . This value is then multiplied by +1 if both the upper and lower bounds have the same sign (i.e., the interval does not include zero), as their product will be positive, or -1 if the upper and lower bounds have different signs (i.e., the interval does include zero), as their product will be negativefoot_0 . For example, the interval [3,4] is 3 units away from 0, has a width of 1, and both values are the same sign, so the 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 = 3 1 ×1 = 3. The interval is 3 CI widths away from zero. Whereas for an interval [-2,4], the minimum distance is 2, width is 6, and sign of the product is -1, so the 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 = 2 6 × -1 = -.33. The RP is somewhat more difficult to interpret when it's negative, but it is useful to note that when a CI is symmetric around zero (e.g., [-2,2]) the RP will be equal to -0.5, which is its minimum possible value.

A positive RP indicates a CI that excludes zero and is thus statistically significant, whereas a negative RP indicates a CI that overlaps with zero and is not statistically significant.

As CIs move further from zero and/or become narrower due to greater precision, RPs grow larger, a phenomenon comparable to the increasing t or z statistics as statistical power improves.

Even a true effect can result in an RP score that is very close to zero due to random chance. However, the likelihood that this occurs across many studies is very low. So, while a single study with a low RP cannot be used to identify a false-positive result, we can aggregate a set of RP scores together to see if there is a pattern of RP scores that are too close to zero, which would indicate a lack of evidential value (Adler, Roseler, & Schoniger, 2023). To provide context, the RP distribution from reported results must be compared to another distribution, which can be either real or simulated data. Götz and colleagues (2021) conducted a variety of statistical simulations demonstrating that RP distributions are sensitive to selection bias (i.e., the selection of results which show positive and strong support for hypotheses) across a variety of effect sizes and standard errors. Additionally, they demonstrated that the RP distributions across five psychology journals show evidence of selection bias, meaning low evidential value.

In our study we focus on validating the RP measure through additional simulation studies and using RP to evaluate published mediation analyses from top marketing and consumer psychology journals. Study 1 demonstrates the effect of specific researcher degrees of freedom on both false-positive rates and RP. These results build on Götz and colleagues (2021) by demonstrating the correspondence between RP and false positives as well as examining which specific practices in mediation analyses have the greatest impact on evidential value. In Study 2, we extract RP values from published mediation analysis in four top marketing and consumer psychology journals, comparing the distribution to simulated values to evaluate existing evidential value of mediation results in marketing and consumer psychology.

Study 1: Exploring the Impact of Researcher Degrees of Freedom

The purpose of Study 1 is to explore the impact of analytical flexibility (i.e., researcher degrees of freedom) on the false-positive error rates and RP distributions of indirect tests. We simulated analytical flexibilities that are specific to mediation analysis to evaluate how each practice impacts the false-positive error rate and RP distribution.

In their seminal paper, Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) introduced the field of psychology to the concept of researcher degrees of freedom (RDFs). The authors used Monte Carlo simulations to demonstrate how flexibility in choice of the outcome variable, sample size, covariates, and conditions (as well as the combination of these practices) inflate false-positive error rates. The original authors focused on main effects in a two-condition design, and their results emphasized how common practices in the field lead to surprisingly high false-positive error rates. Researchers practicing in marketing and psychology need to consider similar issues with currently common practices in mediation analysis. Our focus in this simulation are RDFs which are specific to mediation analysis and especially those that have been advocated by researchers in the field.

Specifically, we consider swapping the role of variables in the analysis (mediators and outcomes), choosing among candidate mediators and outcomes, testing moderation of different paths in the mediation analysis, including or excluding a covariate, trying multiple inferential methods for testing the indirect effect, and rerunning resampling procedures. We examine two primary outcomes: false-positive error rate and distribution of the RP index. We assume that RDFs have consequences of different severity on these indicators.

We simulate data under varied null hypotheses, where either the a-path or the b-path is zero and the other path varies in its magnitude. The direct effect is fixed at 0 throughout the simulationsfoot_1 . Sample size is fixed to 224, which was the median sample size in the studies examined in Study 2. In each condition, 2,000 simulations are run, and when resampling/bootstrapping procedures are used they have 1,000 resamples.

Study 1: Hypotheses

We expected that under the null-hypothesis, each RDF will increase false-positive error rate and result in a higher RP index distribution. Among the different RDFs, we expect multiple inferential methods and rerunning bootstraps to have the smallest effects on false-positive error rates (i.e., they are relatively ineffective methods for p-hacking). Based on Hayes and Scharkow's (2013) agreement among inferential methods tends to be relatively high, and so we expect trying multiple inferential methods will not affect false-positive error rates very much.

Similarly, bootstrap confidence intervals should be relatively stable with 1,000 resamples, so repeating them is unlikely to result in a large inflation of false-positive errors. By contrast we hypothesized that choosing among candidate mediators and outcomes and testing moderation will result in the highest false-positive error rates. These two decisions increase the number of available tests the most, presenting the greatest opportunity for inflated false-positive error rates.

Study 1: Methods

All data and code are available at https://osf.io/25rwy/?view_only=b91e790f23f046cf813e0c508fb72d06 [Note: Anonymized for peer review, will be updated upon acceptance].

Data generation

Data was generated such that the independent variable X is a random normal variable with mean zero and standard deviation of 1. The mediator was generated using Equation 2and the standard deviation of the residuals is set to √1 -𝑎𝑎 2 which fixes the population variance of the mediator to 1, leading to the desired standardized effect size. The outcome variable is generated using Equation 3 with the direct effect (𝑐𝑐′) fixed at zero and the standard deviation of the residuals set to √1 -𝑎𝑎 2 which fixes the population variance of the outcome to 1, leading to the desired standardized effect size. The effect sizes for the non-zero path were set to 0.14, 0.39 or 0.59, conforming to previous simulation research in mediation analysis (e.g., Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007; Hayes & Scharkow, 2013; Yzerbyt et al., 2018; Montoya, 2022) and aligning with Cohen's small, medium, and large standardized effect sizes (Cohen, 1988). Regression equations aligning with our method of generating data were as follows:

Analysis

For the analysis with no RDFs, the coefficients were estimated using two linear regressions.

Then 1,000 bootstrap resamples were used to generate a 95% percentile bootstrap confidence interval for the indirect effect. The first row of results in Table 1 reports the proportion of significant results, thus the proportion of false-positive results (the 95% CI of the indirect effect does not include zero) with no RDFs. To estimate how RDFs affect this error rate, we explored the variations in the rows below mimicking as closely as possible a researcher's process. We explore variations of the analysis separately and record the proportion of false-positive findings and retain the largest relative proximity. Across all methods, the largest relative proximity was selected among all analyses and the original analysis (no RDF). If any of the analyses result in a significant indirect effect, a false-positive is recorded.

Swapping M and Y.

A second mediation analysis was fit which switches the mediator and the outcome in the analysis. We record the largest RP of the two models (original and swapped), and whether the recorded result is significant.

Choices of M and Y (2 of each) (r = .5). We generated a second mediator to have a correlation with the first mediator of .5, and we generated a second outcome to have a correlation with the first outcome of .5. This allows for nine possible mediation models to be fit: if the no RDF model or any of the above models had a significant 95% bootstrap confidence interval as well as the largest RP.

Testing Moderation.

A moderator is generated as a balanced dichotomous variable (50% is 0, and 50% is 1). This variable is then tested in a moderated mediation model corresponding to PROCESS models 7, 8, 14, 15, 58, and 59 (Hayes, 2022; See Figure 2). We calculated two possible false-positive rates from these analyses, the first is if there is a significant index of moderated mediation in any of the models (IMM only), and second is if there is a significant index of moderated mediation or the conditional indirect effect is significant at either of the two values of the moderator (IMM and Conditional IE). The index of moderated mediation is a value that measures the degree of linear moderation of the indirect effect, and similar to indirect effects is the product of two coefficients from separate regression models (Hayes, 2015). through M is moderated by W. Each model allows W to moderate a different path or set of paths.

Model numbers correspond to those from the PROCESS macro (Hayes, 2022).

Covariate Inclusion/Exclusion.

A covariate is generated as a balanced dichotomous variable (the same way as the moderator). This variable is then entered into the model as a covariate in the model for M, the model for Y, and a covariate in the models for M and Y, leading to four potential models from a single covariate (no covariate [no RDF model], covariate for M only, covariate for Y only, covariate for M and Y). The largest RP is recorded, and if any of the models result in a significant indirect effect (95% percentile bootstrap CI), then a false positive is recorded.

Multiple Inferential Methods.

There are many inferential methods available for mediation.

Given a single set of data we use 6 inferential methods: percentile bootstrap confidence intervals (no RDF model), bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals, bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap confidence intervals, the Sobel test (first-degree and second-degree Taylor expansions), and Monte Carlo confidence intervals (using 1,000 samples) 3.

Rerunning Resampling (20 times).

The final RDF is explored by rerunning the bootstrapping procedure (i.e., percentile bootstrap confidence intervals) 20 times, and if any of the 20 confidence intervals exclude zero this is recorded as a false-positive result and the largest RP is recorded. The first sample is the no RDF model and 19 additional samples are generated.

Study 1: Results

In this section we summarize the results of the simulation study, discussing first the results for false positives then the results for RP distribution. Overall the simulation shows that the explored RDFs do indeed increase false-positive error rates, and differentially so across practices. The distribution of RP is similarly perturbed in line with the patterns of false positives. This builds on the work from Götz and colleagues (2021) demonstrating the validity of RP as a diagnostic for evidential value in mediation analysis.

False-positive Error Rates

Table 1 displays the false-positive error results for each RDF at each effect size condition. First examining the no RDF condition, false-positive error rates are well controlled and close to .05 when the non-zero path is sufficiently large, and somewhat conservative (less than .05) when the non-zero path is small. This result is in line with many prior simulations in mediation analysis (Hayes & Scharkow, 2013; Biesanz et al., 2010; MacKinnon et al., 2004).

The most innocuous RDF was covariate inclusion/exclusion (False-positive rate range .0265 -.0555). False positives were not particularly inflated under this method, though it was always greater than the no researcher degree of freedom condition. Notably, the covariate was generated to be independent of all of the other variables in the model, to be consistent with the idea that this variable is unnecessary. Whereas, if the covariate was correlated with the variables in the model, it could be viewed as a confounder, and then should be included in the model. The choice to keep the covariate independent, may have resulted in very limited impact on falsepositive rate. Results may differ with covariates which are correlated with other variables in the mediation model.

Multiple inferential methods and rerunning bootstraps had a non-trivial but generally small effect on false-positive error rates (.0530 -.0705 and .0365 -.0805, respectively).

Similarly, swapping M and Y has a somewhat small effect (.0250 -.0900), yet it was notable that this seemed to have more of an effect when the a-path was zero compared to when the b-path was zero. When the b-path is nonzero, swapping M and Y maintains that relationship on the bpath while giving a "second chance" to the a-path. Whereas when the b-path is zero, swapping M and Y result in minimal change in the results.

There were a few approaches that inflated false-positive error rates to unacceptable levels: choices of M and Y (.0455 -.1940) and testing moderated mediation with either the index of moderated mediation (.0515 -.1480) or the conditional indirect effects (.0755 -.2040).

Notably, both of these estimates could be underestimating the impact these options have in real research. In real research, researchers could test more variables, leading to even higher error rates. We only allowed for two options for M and two options for Y whereas real research may have many more options. Similarly, for moderated mediation we only looked at one possible moderator. In practice, these false-positive error rates could be much higher.

Overall our hypotheses were confirmed: rerunning bootstraps, inferential methods, and covariates were the least impactful practices; whereas, choices of variables and moderated mediation inflate false-positive error rates the most. While these results shed light on the potential impact of these research practices on the evidential value of mediation analysis, they can also provide additional support for the validity of the RP index, which is a relatively new statistic. We can assess how these RDFs impact the distribution of the RP and whether the results are aligned with those seen for false positives. If the outcomes are aligned this suggests that RP can operate as a valid proxy for examining false positives within contexts very closely aligned to those in the simulation (i.e., specific to mediation analysis).

Relative Proximity

Figure 3 provides a visual depiction of the distribution of the relative proximity under each of the data generating and RDF conditions. The primary features of this graph show that the RDFs that most strongly impacted false positives (Choice of M and Y and Moderated Mediation) shift the RP distribution right relative to the no RDF distributions. For the practices that impacted false positives least (covariates, inferential method, and rerunning bootstraps) the distributions look most similar to the no RDF condition. Just as was seen with the false positives, the difference between RP distributions when a is nonzero vs. when b is nonzero, mirrors the differences we observed with false-positive rates. Overall, this demonstrates that when RDFs are utilized, this will manifest in the distribution of the RP, specifically in a shift of the distribution right, toward more positive values.

Figure 4 visualizes the relationship between average RP and false positives for each condition in the simulation. This visualization shows the very close correspondence between these two measures. It also emphasizes how the correspondence between RP and false-positive rate differs when the non-zero parameter is very small. Previous research has shown that falsepositive rates are overly conservative in these conditions (Biesanz et al., 2001; Hayes & Scharkow, 2013). RP does not seem to suffer from the same problem, but this should be studied more specifically, as this was not the primary goal of this particular study.

Study 1: Discussion

Study 1 is a Monte Carlo simulation that demonstrates how different RDFs can impact false positives and relative proximity in mediation analysis. Overall, we find very close correspondence between the RP and false positives, suggesting the RP may serve as a reliable index by which to evaluate the evidential value of published mediation literature. Notably, RP has not been evaluated for contexts outside of mediation. Additionally, we identified specific practices which have a large impact on false-positive rates: choice of mediators and outcomes and testing moderated mediation. These practices suggest that preregistration of mediation (and moderated mediation) analysis is recommended to provide transparency about whether specific mediation models were hypothesized a priori. In the next study we apply the RP statistic to evaluate empirical mediation results from marketing and consumer psychology publications to assess the evidential value of the published literature. IMM = Index of Moderated Mediation, IE = Indirect Effect. Study 2: Comparing Marketing and Consumer Psychology Journals to Simulated

Data

The purpose of Study 2 was to test how RP scores calculated from mediation analyses reported in marketing and consumer psychology journals compared to data simulated under a variety of population conditions. To this end, we simulated three different RP distributions (low power, adequate power, and null effects). The simulated distributions were separately plotted against the marketing and consumer psychology journal distribution so that we could examine the similarity among the four distributions. In this way, we hoped to examine whether the observed data showed the most similarity to adequately powered tests, low-powered tests, null tests, or a mixture of these categories.

Our first step in comparing RP distributions was to collect reported CIs from marketing and consumer psychology journals and convert them to RP scores. The data were compiled from four highly cited marketing and consumer psychology journals, the Journal of Consumer Psychology, the Journal of Consumer Research, the Journal of Marketing and the Journal of Marketing Research during a three-year period (2018-20) 4 . Next, we simulated mediation analyses that were adequately powered (80-95% power), low-powered (33-79% power) and null effects (~5% false-positive rate). We then compared the distribution of RP scores from the mediation analyses to the simulated distributions.

Study 2: Methods

In this section we describe the methods used to collect test statistics from published papers in marketing and consumer psychology journals using mediation analysis. Additionally, we describe how we simulated data to evaluate alignment of RP distributions. Finally, we describe how we compared the observed RP distributions to the simulated distributions. All data and code are available at https://osf.io/25rwy/?view_only=b91e790f23f046cf813e0c508fb72d06 [Note: Anonymized for Peer Review, will be updated upon acceptance].

Collecting Test Statistics from Published Mediation Analyses.

To test the collective evidential value of mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology journals, we conducted a systematic review of reported test statistics. We chose the following high impact journals for our analysis: Journal of Consumer Research (JCR), and

Journal of Consumer Psychology (JCP), Journal of Marketing (JM), and Journal of Marketing

Research (JMR). We selected these journals because they have high impact factors and represent typical outlets for mediation studies in marketing. We analyzed three years of each of the preceding journals, which covered all articles which appeared in print between 2018 and 2020 for each journal. Our initial sample contained 647 publications. Using keywords such as mediation, indirect, Hayes, and PROCESS, a laboratory assistant and the fourth author manually reviewed each article to identify those containing at least one mediation model with accompanying CI. This initial screening of publications resulted in a sample of 308 publications. During analysis, we excluded and additional 13 publications which contained multilevel models (6), were repeated-measures designs (2), were retracted (2), were non-linear mediation models (1), or were in retrospect found not to contain any mediation model ( 2). An additional ten papers were unusable because they lacked a codable CI. This process resulted in a final dataset of 285 mediation analyses.

The articles that included mediation were then given to a team of six laboratory assistants who were trained to manually code mediation analyses, but naive to the hypotheses. We chose to apply manual harvesting of test statistics rather than mechanical harvesting because research articles tend to include many test statistics that are not central to the core hypotheses and therefore less informative regarding problems with evidence quality (Simonsohn et al., 2014).

Working independently, pairs of assistants were instructed to record the first reported hypothesized test of an indirect effect mentioned in the publication subject to two exceptions. If the first reported test was to rule out alternative explanations, the assistants were told to ignore these tests in favor of tests which were hypothesized. In the case of moderated mediation, the assistants were told to record the index of moderated mediation, if it was reported, even if it was not reported before any other indirect effects.

The selected articles were manually coded, to record the first reported hypothesized test of an indirect effect mentioned in the publication, the hypothesis test, the point estimates of the indirect effect or the index of moderated mediation, its standard error and/or the CIs around the point estimate, as well as the formal hypothesis on which the test was based. If reported, further details about the component paths in the mediation model, such as point estimates, effect sizes (group means and standard deviations), or inferential statistics (F-test or t-test) were recorded along with other details about the estimation (the confidence level of the interval, the model number of the PROCESS macro used, and what kind of interval was calculated, and using how many bootstrap samples). Next, we calculated the RP (Götz et al. 2021) for each mediation analysis of interest by dividing the reported CI's distance to zero by its width (See Eq. 1).

Data simulations

We ran a series of simulations to determine how the RP scores ought to be distributed for simple mediation analyses when adequately powered (80-95% power), low-powered (33-79% power), and null effects (~5% false-positive rate). We used the simstudy::genCorData R function (Goldfield & Wjciak-Jens, 2019) to create each simulated dataset with pre-specified population-level correlations among the three variables (X, the independent variable; M, the mediator, and Y, the outcome variable). To test the simulated indirect effects, we used the mediate function from the psych package for R (Revelle, 2015) with default options (alpha = .05; 5,000 bootstraps; percentile CIs). We verified that this tool gives results consistent with the PROCESS macro (Hayes, 2022). Just like with the test statistics collected from marketing and consumer psychology journals, RP scores were calculated using Equation 1.

To simulate the adequate and low powered true effects, we used a weak population-level indirect effect (ab=.04) and a residual direct effect of zero. We selected ab=.04 because it allowed us to achieve desired power levels using sample sizes that are similar to those reported in marketing and consumer psychology journals and is in-line with previous meta-analyses of mediation (Götz et al., 2021; Aberson, 2019b). We considered three possible population models: the X-M correlation is equal to the M-Y correlation (rXM = .20, rMY = .20, rXY = .04), the X-M correlation is four times the size of the M-Y correlation (rXM = .4, rMY = .1, rXY = .04), and the X-M correlation is one quarter of the M-Y correlation (rXM = .1, rMY = .4, rXY = .04).

The means and standard deviations of X, M, and Y were always 0 and 1, respectively.

We manipulated power by varying the sample size of each simulated data set while holding all other parameters constant. Sample sizes were drawn at random, uniformly, from a range based on Monte Carlo estimates (Schoemann et al., 2017) for adequate power (See Table 2). For null effects, we ran simple mediation analyses on a series of simulated 3-variable data sets in which all population correlations among variables was set to zero except one path (apath or b-path), which was assigned to have weak (.1), moderate (.3), strong (.5; Cohen, 1988), or very strong correlations (.7). Simulated sample sizes were varied based on 20th, 40th, 60th, and 80th percentile sample sizes reported in the published mediation analysis sample (N = 138, 195, 250, and 335 respectively). These 2 (Null path) x 4 (strength) x 4 (Sample Size) = 32 different combinations were used to simulate the heterogeneity in a realistic null distribution and to assess whether there are meaningful differences among null distributions.

All simulations were designed such that the RP > 0 peak of their respective RP distributions matched the peak of the marketing and consumer psychology journals' RP distribution. 5 This allowed us to compare the shapes of the simulated and observed distributions directly using absolute frequencies. In our final simulated distributions, mediation analyses reached statistical significance in 87% (a<b), 89% (a=b), and 89% (a > b) of tests designed to simulate adequate power, 58% (a<b), 60% (a=b), and 60% (a > b) of tests simulating low power.

For the null effects the false-positive rates varied by the magnitude of the non-zero path, similar to Study 1 and prior simulation findings (MacKinnon et al., 2004; Yzerbyt et al., 2018; Biesanz 5 We programmed all sets of simulations to run until the highest positive point of each of their respective RP histograms was 1,000 units for a bin width of .05 (7,252 tests of adequate power, 6,769 tests of lower power and 54,574 tests of null effects).
