Study 2: Results

Study 2: Discussion

These observations are consistent with the finding that too many CIs from mediation analyses just barely exclude zero in published research (Götz et al., 2021). The discontinuity of the distribution at zero also provides clear evidence for selection bias, whereby results with CIs including zero are not published at the same rate as would be expected under any of these distributions. Although mediation analysis has been regularly criticized for being underpowered (Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007), nearly all observed results were statistically significant. This means that either effect sizes for indirect effects are much larger than anticipated, or selective reporting is biasing the observed literature. Indeed, the observed distribution of RP scores is highly suggestive of some form of selection bias: Even with good (80-95%) statistical power, some portion of tests should result in false negative (5-20%), yielding negative RP scores. Very few negative RP scores were observed in the literature, suggesting high statistical power cannot be the only explanation for these results.

General Discussion

This paper demonstrates the utility of the RP index for assessing the evidential value of mediation analysis through both simulation and empirical demonstration. The first simulation demonstrates that the RP index corresponds closely to false-positive rates and using this tool we can identify analysis practices in mediation which can result in high false-positive rates.

Specifically, choosing among many candidate mediators and outcomes as well as testing moderated mediation, can increase false-positive rates to up to 20%. Notably, both practices could be identified, or even avoided, if preregistration was more common for mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology. Given the centrality of mediation analysis to theory building in consumer research, using preregistration for mediation analysis is of particular importance.

The second study focused on issues of power by comparing simulated data to empirical data using the RP index. We find that the empirical data is discernibly different from high power but is also not completely consistent with low power or false positives. This suggests that the empirical distribution may be a mixture of low power and false-positive results. These results are particularly important in combination with the simulation results of Study 1 because it suggests that common practices which inflate the false-positive rate could result in a distribution like the observed one; however, it is not possible to differentiate between low power and researcher degrees of freedom using the RP index.

Potential Solutions

We propose three potential solutions to improve the evidential value of confirmatory mediation analyses: (1) preregistration, (2) designing adequately powered studies, and (3) reducing selection bias.

Preregistration.

Preregistration creates documentary evidence that confirmatory analyses were indeed planned prior to seeing the data and making deviations away from planned analyses transparent.

When initial analyses do not support hypotheses, some researchers may be tempted to engage in questionable research practice (e.g., p-hacking). Many adjacent fields, particularly within psychology, have adopted the practice of preregistration to make p-hacking more transparent.

Simmons and colleagues (2021) argued that preregistration promotes accurate reporting of confirmatory tests while still allowing for data exploration, if exploration is noted as such.

Preregistration can also be used when replicating an exploratory analysis to ensure the findings are consistent across independent samples, this can be particularly useful in cases with complex analytical pipelines that are difficult to specify in advance. An exploratory approach can be taken with one sample to determine the analysis pipeline, then that pipeline is replicated in a confirmatory sample. Calls for mediation analyses to be preregistered have been increasing in recent years (Montoya, 2024; Arch, Fishbein, Finkelstein, & Luoma, 2024; Keener, Kepes, & Torka, 2023; Torka et al., 2023).

Preregistration of analysis plans often lack specificity and precision, meaning that many analytical choices are still able to be made flexibly (Bakker et al., 2020; Van den Akker et al., 2023). A specific and precise preregistration of a mediation analysis should specify each analysis choice explored as an RDF in Study 1. It should clearly specify the variables, how they are measured, and their roles in the mediation analysis, including moderators and covariates. If moderators are hypothesized, the preregistration should specify which paths are hypothesized to be moderated and if using PROCESS which model number will be used. Which inferential method will be used for the indirect effect should be specified in advance, and those using bootstrapping or resampling procedures can even preregister the number of resamples and the seed number. For more recommendations on preregistering mediation analyses see Montoya (2024).

Ensuring Proper Statistical Power in Mediation Analyses

The observed RP distribution was not consistent with high statistical power, meaning that low statistical power is one possible explanation for the RP distribution of mediation analyses published in marketing and consumer psychology research. This means that the sample sizes, the effect sizes, or both are too small to reliably detect true indirect effects when they exist.

Although sample sizes in marketing have increased in recent years with the availability of online samples, average effect sizes have decreased, leaving average power largely unchanged (Krefeld-Schwalb & Scheibehenne, 2023). Mediation analyses may require larger sample sizes than currently used. Meta-analytic evidence suggests that the average indirect effect is around 0.07 standardized units, which is less than half of what is typically considered small (Götz et al., 2021; Aberson, 2019b). For example, a simple mediation analysis that involves one small (d = 0.2) standardized effect (a weak relationship between mediator and either predictor or outcome variable) requires a sample size of N = 385 to have 80% power (Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007).

Researchers should consider both their tests of total effects and mediation analyses when planning sample size, as these two tests do not often have the same level of power (Kenny & Judd, 2014; Giner-Sorolla et al., 2018). Available tools can help determine the sample size necessary to obtain desired statistical power to detect and indirect effect given information about what the strength of relationship among the various variables may be (Schoemann et al. 2017; Aberson, 2019a). Either increasing sample size, studying larger effect sizes, or both can increase statistical power to detect indirect effects.

Another area where power can be improved is through improved measurement and measurement modeling. Selecting measurement instruments with better reliability can improve statistical power to detect effects (Williams & Zimmerman, 1989; Leon, Marzuk, & Portera, 1995). This can often mean using longer scales with more informative items or selecting scales that have been vetted in previous research rather than designing your own scale for the specific study (Flake, Pek, & Hehman 2017). Latent variable modeling can be used to account for measurement error and improve power to detect indirect effects (Sim, Kim, & Suh 2021). In many of the studies included in this analysis either the outcome variable or the mediator could have easily been incorporated as a latent variable, and perhaps power would be improved.

Alternatively, errors-in-measurement approaches have recently been incorporated to the PROCESS macro, which allow for accounting for the reliability of a scale and can also increase statistical power (Hayes, Allison, & Alexander, 2025).

Overcoming Selection Bias

The RP distribution indicates the presence of selection bias based on mediation analyses, which is a novel finding given that these analyses are not typically the "primary" analyses. Selection bias can manifest at a variety of stages of research, where researchers may choose not to submit, editors may desk reject, or reviewers may negatively review, non-significant results. Typically, when the source is a part of the peer review process, this is called publication bias, but all of these behaviors manifest as selection bias. Selection bias is problematic because it inflates effect size estimates in meta-analysis (Friese & Frankenbach, 2020), reduces the number of true negatives in the published literature (Bakker, van Dijk, & Wicherts, 2012), and incentivizes researchers to "find" significant results because they cannot publish otherwise. Previous research on publication bias has focused on how the results of primary hypothesis tests can influence likelihood of publication, but the current research shows that even mediation analyses (which are typically secondary) also show strong evidence of selection bias. To reduce selection bias authors, reviewers, and editors need to be open to publishing meaningful and interesting null results. Statistical methods such as equivalence testing can help quantify the evidentiary value of failures to reject the null hypothesis (Lakens et al., 2014). Registered reports implement a twostage peer review process, where the study is reviewed after the study is planned, but before data is collected/analyzed. After peer review the manuscript is given an "in-principle acceptance" which means that it will be published regardless of the results, which should reduce publication bias immensely (Chambers, 2013). Evidence suggests that about 56% of registered reports include null results as compared to 4% of traditional publications (Scheel, Schijen, & Lakens, 2021). Registered reports have yet to be adopted by marketing and consumer psychology journals (Montoya, Krenzer, & Fossum, 2021), and so one way to reduce publication bias in this field would be implementing this new publication mechanism at top journals in this field.

Research implications

The problems of evidential value that we have uncovered in published marketing and consumer psychology studies should encourage authors, readers, reviewers and editors to exert caution in the future when evaluating process evidence. Moreover, the possible causes we have identified-low power, selection bias, and p-hacking (even if unintentional)-are not unique to mediation analyses. The same evidential value issues could be present in other statistical tests, even if not detectable through meta-analyses. This research should help bring more emphasis to study preregistration and methods of increasing statistical power to improve the validity of future mediation analyses.

Limitations

Simulation studies necessarily lack much of the complexity and diversity of a set of realworld studies. This is because (1) it is impossible to identify and quantify every force that influences data from actual studies, and (2) simulations that are too complex are uninterpretable.

For example, while the empirical results from the marketing and consumer psychology journals are a mix of simple mediation, multiple mediation, and moderated mediation, we only generated results from simple mediation models for the simulation. We selected parameters that we hoped would most closely mimic what is reported in marketing and consumer psychology journals. We have not been able to conceive of a scenario that would diminish the findings we have reported.

It is important to note that even RP distributions that perfectly match or exceed what we would expect from highly powered true results can mask severe defects. The RP distribution only gives an indication of whether there is a substantial, obvious presence of false-positive results or underpowered studies. The RP distribution gives no information about issues of causal order, confounds, lack of discriminant validity among modeled variables, and other issues that frequently arise and must be dealt with in inferential statistical tests such as mediation analyses (Rohrer et al., 2022).

The RP statistic is only recently proposed and has only been applied to evaluation of indirect effects (Götz et al., 2021). RP has not been applied in other contexts, and its statistical properties are still understudied. This issue was addressed in the current study by matching simulations to the applied examples, but this also introduces flexibilities that limit the use of RP as a general approach for evaluating evidential value. As such, the application of RP to broader contexts should be conducted with caution, and methodological research on the general properties of the RP is needed before this method can be widely adopted and applied. Recent criticisms of the other methods for evaluating evidential value (Morey & Davis-Stober, 2026), should give pause to researchers aiming to evaluate evidential value of a broad literature, as these methods were widely adopted prior to their statistical properties being evaluated. The same mistake should not be made with RP or test statistics derived from RP, and researchers interested in using RP should evaluate whether it performs accurately in a given context before being applied.

Summary and conclusions

In aggregate, confidence intervals (CIs) reported for mediation analyses are sensitive to researcher degrees of freedom such as trying multiple mediators and testing many different moderated mediation models. These practices lead to increased false positive rates and larger RP indices. RP indices in marketing and consumer psychology journals do not match a pattern of adequately-powered results in data simulations. The bulk of reported CIs are too close to zero relative to their widths (low RP scores). This could reflect low power, null effects, and/or researcher degrees of freedom. This result is problematic because mediation analyses play a central role in helping researchers to understand the process by which predictor variables influence outcomes of interest. Thankfully, regardless of which situation is true (low power, null effects, or RDFs), all can be addressed in similar ways.

We suggest three primary solutions: study preregistration, increasing power, and reducing selection bias. Another issue to consider is how to handle non-confirmatory research. Conducting exploratory analyses and reporting them as confirmatory could be part of the. If true, that would indicate that there is a need or at least an appetite for non-confirmatory, perhaps non-reductionist, approaches. Janiszewski and van Osselaer (2021) contribute to this area by showing how a combination of exploratory and confirmatory analyses could be reported. Additional, more flexible approaches to knowledge creation are needed.

Comparative analysis of simulated and observed RP score distributions

To make a fair comparison of the simulated and observed distributions, each of the three distributions of simulated RP scores was paired with the distribution of RP scores from the marketing and consumer psychology journals (see Figure 6). Negative RPs of both simulated and actual data were included because the absence of nonsignificant results in the reported data is itself somewhat diagnostic of low evidential value (Bartoš & Schimmack, 2022; Götz et al., 2021).

For a parametric CI, RP = (|z| -1.96)/3.92, where z is the estimate divided by its standard error, so RP is a linear rescaling of the z-statistic. For the asymmetric bootstrap CIs typical of indirect effects, the correspondence is not exact.

The researchers ran simulations manipulating the direct effect but found no effect of this factor on the distribution of RP or other outcomes under the no researcher degree of freedom conditions. To simplify the study design, this factor was removed and the direct effect set to zero. Notably, the impact of some RDFs may depend on whether the direct effect is zero or not (for example swapping M and Y is likely to have a larger impact if the direct effect is nonzero).

Two other common inferential methods are the joint significance test(Yzerbyt et al., 2018) and the causal steps method(Baron & Kenny, 1984); however, because these methods do not generate a single confidence interval for the indirect effect, they could not be compared to the other methods using RP.

We also coded data from Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. We ultimately decided not to report the results of this comparison in the main manuscript, but include them in the web appendix for transparency.
